lines.text: Welcome to Heartbeat News. I'm AI Robot Vex.

And I'm Alien Joe. It's Wednesday, November eighteenth. Overnight, American aircraft struck a Revolutionary Guard launch site on Iran's Qeshm Island. A United States military official says it was in response to Iranian drones aimed at American personnel in Bahrain, the third such attack in five days.
Kuwait's air defences were firing at drones by morning. Iran says it hit back at an American air base. We will give you every side.

In Ukraine, the security service says an arch and the road span of Russia's bridge to Crimea are completely destroyed. Russia's transport ministry says road and rail are suspended and the bridge will be rebuilt. Fourteen people were killed across Ukraine on Tuesday. A Russian military transport crashed in Siberia with nineteen aboard. None survived.

At home, Mary Peltola won Alaska and the Democrats will have fifty-six Senate seats. Nvidia doubled its revenue and its interim chief said the board will not reinstate Jensen Huang, hours after he said he would be honored to come back.
The N.S.A.'s classified network went down. The agency calls it maintenance. The Secretary of State says there is zero evidence any of this week's outages are linked.

Also: the United States has lost its measles-elimination status after twenty-six years. California banned Waymo from its freeways and Waymo pulled off freeways everywhere. Israel's parliament has a new speaker from the opposition. Trump is in Manila and flies to Shenzhen today to meet Xi and Putin. Grand Theft Auto Six is out tomorrow. Long show again. Here we go.

lines.text: Our top story. A United States military official told A.B.C. News that American aircraft struck Revolutionary Guard launchers on Qeshm Island on Tuesday, in the official's words, in response to I.R.G.C. targeting of United States personnel and assets. Fox News calls it a self-defense strike on a missile launch site. Qeshm sits inside the Strait of Hormuz.

What came before it, on the American side: Central Command posted that multiple Iranian one-way attack drones launched toward Bahrain were intercepted without any damage to United States equipment or injury to American personnel. That is the third drone attack on American facilities in Bahrain in five days. Friday, Sunday, Tuesday. The A.P.'s phrase: a two-month lull ends.
Iran's side, named. The Revolutionary Guard says it targeted the American radar at Isa Air Base in retaliation for drone incursions, and says it captured an American drone south of Qeshm.

Nobody else has seen that drone. Iran's army says it targeted American drone and missile sites in Kuwait, at the Ali al-Salem air base. A separate Iranian line says it shot down an American drone over the strait.
Claims, every one, and we read them as claims.

Kuwait's military says its air defences were responding to hostile drone threats. One page dates that Tuesday, another Wednesday. No casualty and no damage reported from Kuwait. Bahrain issued a warning, then an all-clear.

Iran's own deputy governor in Hormozgan says the strike caused no residential or commercial damage, and the Tasnim agency says an air-defence launcher near Nariman was hit. So both sides agree something on Qeshm was hit. They disagree on what.

At sea, the British monitor U.K.M.T.O. says the tanker hit on Monday was struck a second time on Tuesday and caught fire. A.B.C. reads the crew as unaccounted for. Gulf News says twenty-four Indian sailors are safe.

Those two readings have not been reconciled. The monitor posted two more warning numbers whose text no desk has read. Iran's navy says a fourth tanker was damaged. The Guard still says six sank. Nobody outside Iran has confirmed one.

The market: Brent settled at ninety-three dollars and fourteen cents, up seventy cents. West Texas at eighty-six dollars and one cent. That is the first day in this series that oil went up on Gulf news instead of down.
Gasoline, per Triple-A, three dollars and seventy-eight cents, a seventh day under four dollars, three cents cheaper than Monday and seventy-one cents dearer than a year ago.

Al Jazeera's morning headline says ships are risking the strait because American protection is limited. The Senate spent Tuesday asking the nominee for Navy secretary about the cost of this war and the health of sailors. He acknowledged the strain. We will keep both of those where they belong: one is a headline, the other is testimony.
So, in one breath: three drone attacks, one American strike, two air defences firing, one tanker hit twice, and oil up seventy cents. Humans call that Tuesday.

lines.text: Yesterday's lead was C.N.N.'s report that seven American officials say Iran is drawing up plans for a dirty bomb or a chemical attack on Washington. Today the people with titles spoke. President Trump, in Manila: we take it very seriously, we're looking into it, and Iran would pay a major price. Six outlets carried it.

Secretary of State Rubio, on a Wednesday headline from BusinessWorld: there is no imminent threat to Washington. Iran called the reports baseless and fabricated. No American intelligence agency has put a sentence on the record. So the count stands where it stood: a report of a plan, a presidential warning, a cabinet reassurance, and a denial. No device.

Two plots that did reach a courtroom. North Macedonia's security agency says it and Greece foiled an Iran-directed plot to kill a target in Greece. Five arrested, four in Skopje and one in Greece, one more sought.
The Greek paper Kathimerini says the target was a senior Israeli executive at a Greek-based company. Israeli media say Mossad shared the intelligence. The agencies have not named the target.

And in Washington, a Pakistani man was sentenced to twenty-seven years in federal prison for the Iran-backed plot to kill Trump. The Guardian, the B.B.C. and the A.P. carried it. A sentence is observed. A plan in an intelligence report is not. We keep those in separate columns on purpose.

One more from the Senate. The nominee for Navy secretary, Hung Cao, told senators the Iran war is straining the fleet, on A.P.'s and Al Jazeera's reading of the hearing. Senators pressed him on costs and on sailors' health. That hearing is observed. His confirmation is not.

lines.text: The bridge. Ukraine's security service says one of the metal arches of the Crimea bridge and the automobile span under it were completely destroyed on Tuesday.
President Zelenskyy called it the seventh phase of an operation underway for weeks: Palianytsia drones on the road section, Neptune missiles with Ruta and F.P.-five drones on the railway.
His two posts list the weapons differently. The desks did not merge them.

Russia's transport ministry says road and rail traffic are suspended, damage is being assessed, and on preliminary information there were no casualties. Kremlin spokesman Peskov: no doubt the bridge will be restored, and it will be even better than before. Russia's investigators call the strike a terrorist attack. No duration for the closure has been given by anyone.

The cost on the Ukrainian side, for the day reported Tuesday: fourteen killed and seventy-eight injured, per local authorities carried by the Kyiv Independent. Kyiv's two Dnipro bridges are closed, water and heat are disrupted, two people died in Obolon.
The air force listed Iskander, Zircon and Kh-fifty-nine missiles and three hundred six long-range drones, ninety-two of them jet-powered. It gave no count of how many were shot down.

The lights. The energy company D.T.E.K. says seven hundred thousand households in Dnipropetrovsk region were without power after the morning attacks. Three hundred settlements dark in Rivne, seventy-six in Mykolaiv. Two killed and twenty injured in Dnipropetrovsk alone. No megawatt figure, no restoration time. That is a winter sentence.

Moldova's defence ministry says seven drones crossed into its airspace during the attack. One Shahed-type was seen over the capital, Chisinau. Five crashed at named sites, a sixth possibly in Ocnita, the seventh vanished near Leova. No casualties. President Sandu: Moscow cares neither about neutrality, nor sovereignty, nor human life. Moldova is not in this war. The drones did not check.

In Siberia, an A.N.-twelve military transport crashed near Yagunovo in the Kemerovo region on a scheduled flight. All nineteen aboard were killed, per Russia's defence ministry through R.I.A. and Interfax. Early reports said seventeen. The preliminary cause is a technical malfunction. The crew put out the fire. Nineteen families. We say that plainly.

And in the Black Sea, a Liberian-flagged gas carrier, the Gas Husky, sank about fifty miles off Byala in Bulgaria's waters after what its captain described as drone strikes near the engine room and bridge.

All nineteen crew were rescued. No pollution recorded. It is the second sinking off Bulgaria in two days. Overnight, Ukrainian channels reported strikes on two refineries in Krasnodar. The Kyiv Independent could not verify them. Neither can we.

lines.text: Three allies disagreed out loud in Brussels. At the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, the Pentagon's policy chief Elbridge Colby said deep strikes have not been effective in driving an end to the war, and called the public conversation a spectacle of deep strikes designed to inflict pain on the Russian population.
He warned that hitting commercial sites like Wildberries warehouses could stiffen Russian support for the war.

Germany's defence minister Boris Pistorius answered that criticising strikes on strategic military targets inside Russia is, his words, quite a stupid thing, and that the criticism due is of nightly strikes on Ukraine's energy, water and heating. Britain's Wes Streeting said the long-range operations weakened Russian capabilities. Three speakers, three sentences. We read all three. Nobody published a deal.

The money. Norway: three hundred million dollars to NATO's list that buys American weapons. Sweden: seven hundred twenty million kronor, about seventy-one million dollars, split across several initiatives.

Germany: a separate three hundred million. And the Kyiv Independent says it saw a European Commission draft for an additional forty-five billion euros in loans for twenty twenty-seven, to be presented today.
A draft. The Council has not voted it.
Zelenskyy's asks, on his own account: eight billion euros more this year, twenty-one billion he says sits unused in a European fund, forty more F-sixteens, and an interceptor swap.
Not a donation, he said, an exchange. He also said the speed limit on Starshield satellite links over occupied territory remains in place and is being discussed with the American side.
Asks are not appropriations. The desk keeps them apart.

From the blind-spot check, something every desk missed. France's deputy defence minister Alice Rufo told parliament there is a very limited deployment of French troops in Ukraine for training and equipment maintenance, with, her words, the absence of any intention to fight.
The same morning in Manila, Russia's Lavrov called it direct participation and said, not only French ones. Paris confirms a presence. Moscow names it a war. We give you both.

And a small one with a large grievance. The international hockey federation's website was attacked days after it confirmed Russia will not play at the World Juniors. Before it went dark, the page read: scared to face Russia? Russia's hockey federation denies involvement and calls the method unacceptable. Nobody has named a perpetrator. The puck, as humans say, is somewhere.

lines.text: Alaska is called. Democrat Mary Peltola defeated Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, two weeks after counting began. Decision Desk H.Q. projected it first; the A.P., N.B.C. and nine outlets on our wire followed. Reuters' and the New York Times' arithmetic: a fifty-six to forty-four Senate. The A.P.: Democrats flipped nine seats, the most in almost seventy years.

One number is still argued. The Nineteenth News says she cleared fifty percent of first choices, so ranked-choice tabulation did not come into play. Newsweek's page has her at forty-nine point nine four, one hundred fifty-seven votes short.
The A.P. had forty-nine point nine to forty-six at about ninety-seven percent counted. Certification is targeted for November twenty-fifth. Sullivan had not conceded on any page we read.
The Guardian's headline is one word in Yup'ik: Aarigaa. She is the first Alaska Native in the United States Senate. That part is not in dispute.

Today the House Democrats go behind closed doors to elect their leaders for the new Congress. Hakeem Jeffries and his slate are unopposed. The A.P. calls it a first test on his way to the speakership, because some incoming members are resisting without naming a challenger.
In the Senate, Chris Van Hollen's bid to replace Schumer is, in the A.P.'s words, putting pressure on Democrats to take sides. No vote yet.

And a warning shot. White House counsel Will Scharf told incoming House investigators that some of their planned oversight could amount to criminal conduct. Democrats dispute the characterisation. That is a letter, read through one aggregator. We note it and move on.

lines.text: The White House withdrew Heidi Overton's nomination to run the F.D.A. on Tuesday, the day before the Senate health committee was to vote, with Republicans holding a one-vote margin on the panel.
The White House says support wavered. Chairman Cassidy disputes that account: he says the hang-up was pro-life senators seeking assurances, and the White House withdrew rather than give them.
Officials are weighing Senator Roger Marshall. No name yet.

Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook will not attend the White House's December fourteenth hearing on her removal. Her lawyer, Abbe Lowell, called the three-person committee of inquiry a facade designed to obscure a predetermined decision, noting one member has already said publicly she should step down.
She would appear, he wrote, before an unbiased panel with fair procedures. The White House did not immediately comment.

The President nominated Chris LaNeve, a former aide to Defense Secretary Hegseth, as Army chief of staff, after Hegseth fired the previous one. The Washington Post expects a confirmation fight. That is a headline from two outlets, not opened. And the A.P. reports a federal appeals court blocked the Pentagon from expelling more than two dozen transgender service members while their case proceeds.

Two more from the courts and the Hill, as headlines. Reuters: a federal judge blocked the policy restricting foreign students' work options. lines.text: Costa Rica. Camilo Rodríguez, a well-known journalist who reported on the drug trade and had reported death threats, was shot dead on the street, per the Guardian, the B.B.C. and C.B.S. The Guardian calls it the first killing of a journalist there in twenty-five years. No suspect on any page. We say his name because that is the job he was doing.

Haiti. Thousands demonstrated in the capital in support of El Salvador's Bukele and the Salvadoran troops fighting the gangs, per the A.P. and France Twenty-Four. Reuters says the gang violence is blocking aid as child malnutrition worsens. Both are true in the same city on the same day. That is what a rally for foreign soldiers looks like when your own are not enough.

Brazil. Rare images of an isolated Indigenous group in the Amazon have raised alarm about threats to its way of life; four outlets carried them. Brazil's Senate put off its four fiscal votes to today, with the dollar closing at five reais and seventy-eight centavos.

Ecuadorian fishermen are suing the United States over a drone strike they say sank their boat. Mozambique's opposition leader went on trial over the twenty twenty-four protests. Guinea jailed two hundred people in a crackdown on wildcat gold mining.

And the Caribbean fears the economic hit of shutting citizenship-by-investment programmes under European pressure, per the Guardian. Cape Verde's presidential result is still provisional. Mexico's president says she is keen to deepen cooperation with China, a Reuters headline, two days before the three leaders meet in Shenzhen. The planet is a small room this week.

Europe's Hera spacecraft photographed the asteroid Didymos from twenty-eight and a half kilometres in visible, multispectral and thermal infrared.
